query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting approximately 5 at.% Ti into equiatomic NbMoTaW will induce the formation of an inverted microstructure, featuring a continuous ductile BCC matrix with discrete B2 precipitates, thereby improving room-temperature ductility without significantly compromising the alloy's high-temperature strength or its resistance to irradiation damage.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbMoTaW with a single-phase BCC structure that exhibits excellent high-temperature mechanical properties but poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 at.% Ti by partially replacing one of the constituent elements, aiming to alter the phase formation during solidification and subsequent processing.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed and tested under standard conditions for room-temperature mechanical testing, high-temperature mechanical performance (around 1600 °C), and irradiation exposure conditions relevant to nuclear or fusion applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an inverted microstructure characterized by discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous ductile BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Ti addition is expected to promote a slight ordering during solidification or heat treatment that leads to the precipitation of a B2 phase. These precipitates, when properly distributed, improve grain boundary cohesion and accommodate plastic deformation at room temperature while the matrix retains high-temperature phase stability and resistance to irradiation-induced defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the Ti-modified alloy will exhibit increased room-temperature ductility (e.g., higher compressive/tensile strain to failure), maintain similar yield strength and stability at 1600 °C, and show no significant degradation in irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Untreated, equiatomic NbMoTaW with a single-phase BCC structure that has excellent high-temperature strength and predicted irradiation resistance but very limited ductility at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected for Ti additions around 5 at.%; excessive Ti could lead to an overabundance of the ordered phase, potentially compromising high-temperature performance or altering irradiation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Ti content and processing conditions to consistently achieve the desirable inverted microstructure are uncertain. Additionally, the long-term stability of the microstructure under irradiation requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbMoTaW alloys with varying Ti contents (e.g., 0, 3, 5, and 7 at.%), process them under identical heat treatment conditions, and characterize their microstructures using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Perform mechanical tests at room temperature and at 1600 °C, and simulate irradiation exposure (e.g., via ion-beam irradiation) for each composition.
measurements: Yield strength and other mechanical properties at 1600 °C
Irradiation resistance indicators (e.g., defect density, phase stability post-irradiation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 5 at.% Ti alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared to the untreated alloy, or if it exhibits a marked deterioration in high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance (as measured by the specified tests), then the hypothesis that Ti addition induces the beneficial inverted microstructure is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ].
